claims.text: The GI application describes Kutch Bandhani as an ancient dyeing technique in which cloth is tied in intricate patterns with nails, beads or grain so that dye cannot seep into the tied areas.

quotes.quote: The Kutch Bandhani is an ancient, dyeing technique, wherein the fabric is tied in intricate patterns with the help of nails, beads or grain, which prevents the colour from seeping into the tied areas during dyeing.

claims.text: Bandhani is a tie-dye craft in which many parts of the cloth are tied tightly with thread to resist dyes, creating dot-like puckered designs.

quotes.locator: Textile Embellishment: Bandhani/Tie-dye on Textiles, p. 50
quotes.quote: Bandhani (Figure 1) is the traditional craft of tie-dye whereby patterning on textiles is created by tightly tying multiple parts of the fabric with thread to resist dyes and create dot like puckered designs.
bandhani work (a dyeing technique in which patterns are formed from arrangements of resist-dyed dots)

claims.text: Bandhani in its many variations is identified by light circular or square repeating motifs on a dark ground.

quotes.quote: A tie-dyeing technique used to make patterned fabrics, Bandhani in its many variations is identified by light circular or square-shaped repeating motifs on a dark ground.

claims.text: The word bandhani derives from the Sanskrit verbal root bandh, meaning to bind or tie.

quotes.quote: The ter bandhani is derived from the Sanskrit verbal root bandh ("to bind, to tie").
It derives its name from the Sanskrit word baandh, meaning "to tie,"

claims.text: In Gujarat, bandhani is the name for textiles whose designs are made by tying individual parts of the fabric before dyeing.

quotes.quote: Bandhani is an expression used in Gujarat for textiles where different designs are produced by tying individual parts of the fabric before dyeing.

claims.text: Bandhani is also the name for the little dot created in the centre of a square or circle motif as the dye seeps into the cloth.

quotes.quote: Bandhani, is the name given to the characteristic feature on Indian tie and dye. It refers to the little dot created in the centre of square or circle motifs as the dye seeps into the fabric material.

claims.text: The GI application names intricate designs and Rai Dana, or mustard-seed, dots as what makes Kutch Bandhani products unique.

quotes.quote: The manufacturing process of Kutch Bandhani products of Gujarat, using tie-dye method on the woven fabric, is unique with intricate designs and Rai Dana (Mustard Seed) dots.

claims.text: According to the GI application, the manufacturing process of Kutch Bandhani is cumbersome, time consuming and entirely manual.

quotes.quote: The manufacturing process is so cumber-some and time consuming to make a final product. The entire manufacturing process is manual.

claims.text: The Impart encyclopedia states that bandhani was originally practised by the Khatri community in Sindh and later gained popularity among artisans of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.

mastering dyeing which hitherto was the Khatri community's domain

quotes.quote: Technological advancement and the use of eco-friendly synthetic dyes have caused a change in production time and quantity, resulting in a rise in competition and a reduction in price.

quotes.quote: Mass production of cotton tie-dye fabric for dress materials, Sari, Dupatta, Scarf is done by Khatri community.

claims.text: The GI application says Bhuj is well known for its red bandhani, and that dyeing is carried out extensively there as the water of the area is known to give a particular brightness to reds and maroons.

quotes.quote: The city of Bhuj, located in the Gulf of Kutch, in Gujarat is well known for its red Bandhani.
Dyeing process of Bandhani is carried out extensively in this city, as the water of this area is known to give a particular brightness to colors, specifically reds and maroons.

claims.text: Among the features that make Kutch Bandhani unique, the GI application lists colour brightness from using water from the Gulf of Kutch for dyeing.

quotes.quote: Quality in colour brightness due to usage of water from Gulf of Kutch for dyeing.

quotes.quote: Kutch Bandhani fabric is produced in two regions of Gujarat, namely, Saurashtra and Kutch. In Saurashtra, the Jamnagar city is the city is main producing centre of Kutch Bandhani and where as in Kutch, the Kutch Bandhani is produced across the entire district.

claims.text: Bandhani on cotton for contemporary use is produced in Mandvi, Mundra, Anjar and Bhuj.

quotes.quote: Bandhani on cotton fabric for contemporary use is produced in Mandvi, Mundra, Anjar, and Bhuj.

quotes.quote: Major centres for bandhani textile production include Mandvi, Bhuj, Jamnagar, Porbandar and Rajkot in Gujarat

quotes.quote: Cotton tie and dye for Jat community is produced in Nani-Virani in Lakhpat Taluka by Khatri community.

quotes.quote: Jat women have started using printed Bandhani but, they still use tie and dye Bandhani textiles at marriage and special occasions.

claims.text: Simple motifs such as tra kan, nav kan kadi, chut bhindi and kodi are used for cotton bandhani.

quotes.quote: For cotton Bandhani simple motif are used like tra Kan, nav kan kadi, chut bhindi, kodi etc.

claims.text: Kutch Bandhani is prepared on cotton, silk, wool, georgette, tussar and rayon fabrics.

quotes.quote: The Kutch Bandhani is prepared on cotton, silk, wool, Georgette, Tussar and Rayon fabrics.
Silk, cotton, woollen fabrics are mainly used in this craft.

claims.text: Silk Kutch Bandhani uses gajji silk, georgette, chiffon, chinon, tussar, mulberry silk and cotton silk woven with a cotton warp and silk weft.

quotes.quote: Material used for silk Kutch Bandhani are Gajji silk, Georgette, Chiffon, Chinon, Tussar, mulberry silk, cotton silk, (fabric woven with cotton warp and silk weft).
Materials used for Silk Bandhani are: Gajji Silk, Georgette, Chiffon, Chinon, Tussar, Mulberry Silk, Cotton-Silk, (Fabric woven with cotton warp and silk weft).

claims.text: The fineness of the tying depends on the fineness and texture of the material.

quotes.quote: The fineness of the tying is also dependent on the fineness and texture of the material.
Materials such as silk or muslin, which are lighter and have a more desirable weave, conduce better to precise tying and dyeing.
The finer materials enable more intricate designs, and are therefore higher in cost.

claims.text: The V&A describes gajji as a satin-weave silk, used particularly in Gujarat.

quotes.quote: This tie-dyed length of gajji, a satin-weave silk used particularly in Gujarat

claims.text: Fabric for Kutch Bandhani is procured from outside Kutch, from places that include Madurai, Bangalore, Varanasi, Surat and Jamnagar.

quotes.quote: The Bandhani tie-dye artisans procure fabric from outside Kutch from Surat, Jamnagar and Ahmedabad in Gujarat, Bangalore, Tamil Nadu, and other parts of India.
The raw material for manufacturing Kutch Bandhani is procured from Madurai, Bangaluru, Varanasi, Bhiwandi(Mumbai), Surat, Khambat etc.

claims.text: Silk saris for Kutch Bandhani are procured from Bangalore and are 6 metres long, while dress materials are 2.5 to 3 metres.

quotes.quote: The silk fabrics both Sarees and Dress Materials are procured from Bangalore. The Sarees are 6 metres and the length of Dress Materials ranges from 2.5 metres to 3 metres.

claims.text: Designs are marked on a thick plastic sheet with pinholes, through which an ink of geru and black colour or soot mixed with water seeps onto the cloth.

quotes.quote: The designs are marked out on a thick plastic sheet. Pinholes are made around the pattern. The "printing ink" is a mixture of "geru" and black colour or soot mixed with water. The "ink" seeps through the holes to print the pattern on the cloth.

claims.text: Wooden blocks are the traditional tools for printing bandhani designs, but most dyers now apply the geru with stencils of plastic farma paper.

quotes.quote: While the blocks are the traditional printing tools, most dyers today apply the geru with stencils made of plastic Farma paper.
Traditionally, blocks were used to print the designs, but craftspeople now use stencils made of farma paper, a type of laminated paper.
Traditionally, wooden blocks dipped in "geru" (red oxide mixed with water) were used to print the design, but now, plastic farma paper is used.

claims.text: Cloth that has been bleached, usually thin cotton, silk or wool, is folded twice and its design is marked out in the form of dots.

quotes.quote: The cloth which is bleached, usually thin cotton, silk or wool is folded two times and a design are marked out in the form of dots.

claims.text: The printing paste is of washable direct dyes, and this printing is done to make the designs for the tying work.

quotes.quote: The printing paste is that of direct dyes and can be washable. This printing is done for making designs for tying work.

claims.text: For tying, the cloth is folded into four or more layers, and the rangara, or colourer, marks the layout of the pattern with geru, a burnt sienna mixed with water.

quotes.quote: The cloth is folded into four or more layers for tying. The "rangara" (colourer) marks the lay-out of the pattern with special geru (a burntsienna mixed with water) on the material.

claims.text: The GI application says Gujarati craftsmen prefer to tie with bare hands, without aids like a fingernail or small metal ring, for better flow and no risk of damaging the cloth.

quotes.quote: The Gujarati craftsman prefers to work without any aids like finger nail, small metal ring etc. The reason behind is, the flow is much better when working with bare hands and there is no risk of damaging the cloth.

claims.text: The GI application also describes bandhani as decorated by plucking the cloth with the fingernails into many tiny bindings that form a figurative design.

quotes.quote: Bandhani is a type of tie-dye textile decorated by plucking the cloth with the fingernails into many tiny bindings that form a figurative design.

claims.text: Following the printed pattern, tiny sections of cloth are pinched by hand or raised with a metal ring and bound with strong thread, traditionally by women called bandhanaras.

quotes.quote: As per the printed pattern, tiny sections of cloth are pinched by hand, or raised with a metal ring, and bound with a strong thread - traditionally by women known as bandhanaras.
who raises and pinches the fabric in the marked designs using a pointed small fingernail or metal ring with a pointed tip.

claims.text: The GI application says tying a Kutch Bandhani takes from 4 to 90 days, depending on the design.

quotes.quote: The time taken for tying work varies from 4 to 90 days depending upon the Kutch Bandhani design.

claims.text: The GI application's proof of origin says a metre of Kutch Bandhani cloth can have millions of tiny knots, called bheendi in the local Kutch language.

quotes.quote: One of the important specialties of the Bandhani is that a meter long of cloth can have millions of tiny knots known as "Bheendi" in the local Kutch language.

claims.text: The GI application's method of production says a metre of cloth can have thousands of tiny knots, known as bheendi in the local language.

quotes.quote: A metre length of cloth can have thousands of tiny knots known as 'Bheendi' in the local language.

claims.text: Kutch Bandhani has two styles, one of dots and the other of lines called laheria, a name that comes from lahar, meaning waves.

quotes.quote: There are two different styles of Kutch Bandhani. One has the popular dots and the other has lines called "Laheria". "Laheria" originates from the "lahar" which means waves.

claims.text: For laheria, bleached white or yellow-dyed cloth is rolled and tied with thick thread wound at intervals of about an inch, a long stick helping to tie it tightly.

quotes.quote: It is tied in a similar design of thin lines gradually flowing into thicker lines. The tying process is usually done on bleached white cloth or cloth which is dyed yellow.
The cloth is rolled and tied with a thick thread which is wound at an interval of about an inch. The thread is wound on a long stick, which enables them to tie thread tightly on the cloth.

claims.text: The GI application says laheria tying work is mainly carried out by women and girls.

quotes.quote: The thread is wound on a long stick, which enables them to tie thread tightly on the cloth. This work is mainly carried out by women and girls.

claims.text: After tying, the cloth is taken for dyeing, where it is first bleached and rinsed in several tubs of water and then dyed in another colour.

quotes.quote: After the tying process, tied cloth is taken for dyeing. It is bleached First, and then rinsed in several tubs of water. Then it is dyed in another colour.

claims.text: To dye, the desired amount of chemicals is put in a piece of cloth and swirled in hot water, and the cloth is then swirled in it with a wooden stick.

quotes.quote: The desired amount of chemicals are put in a piece of cloth and swirled in hot water, then the cloth is put in the water and swirled around with the help of wooden stick.

claims.text: Once the desired shade is reached the cloth is rinsed in several tubs of water, and the process continues until the desired colour combination is achieved.

quotes.quote: After the desired shade is achieved it is removed and rinsed in several tubs of water. The process continues till the desired colour combination is achieved.

claims.text: Dyeing may be repeated for each colour in the pattern, starting with the lightest shade, with the cloth tied again after a dyeing when needed.

quotes.quote: This process may be repeated multiple times for each colour included in the pattern, starting with the lightest shade.
The dyer always starts with the lightest colour (usually yellow), sends the fabric to be tied again if needed, and repeats the process until all the desired colours have been added.
If there are two colours, the pattern is tied again after the first dye, and then dyed again.

claims.text: A border is coloured by wrapping the gathered tied cloth tightly in plastic bound with a rubber strip and scrubbing the dye into the material by hand.

quotes.quote: Colouring of the border involves another technique. The tied cloth is gathered and tightly wrapped in plastic, and wound over tightly by a rubber strip. The dye is manually scrubbed into the material taking care that wrapped areas does not come into contact with the dye.

claims.text: Vat and naphtha dyes are used for cotton and acid dyes for silk.

quotes.quote: Vat and Naphtha dyes are used for cotton and Acid dyes are used for silk clothes.

claims.text: Earlier, most Kutch Bandhani cloth was the maroon of alizarin derived from madder, with black or brown from various very expensive plants.

quotes.quote: Earlier, most Kutch Bandhani cloth was maroon colour of alizarin derived from madder and black or brown derived from various plants which are very expensive.

claims.text: Dyeing with vegetable dyes requires more time and more water.

quotes.quote: The process using vegetable dyes requires more time and more use of water.

claims.text: Bright colours are expensive and difficult to produce, but synthetic dyes are affordable.

quotes.quote: Bright colours are expensive and difficult to produce but synthetic dyes are affordable.

claims.text: The GI application states that the colours used in Kutch Bandhani are natural, making the best colour combinations possible.

quotes.quote: The colours used in the process are natural and hence best colour combinations are possible.

claims.text: Chemical colours are never used directly, because crystals could get caught in the material and damage it.

quotes.quote: Chemical colours are never used directly, as some crystals could get caught in the material and may damage the material.

claims.text: Fast dyes that can be applied cold make it possible to dye individual parts by hand with a piece of felt tied round a wooden handle.

quotes.quote: With the discovery of fast dyes which can also be applied cold, it has become possible to dye individual parts by hand with piece of felt which is tied round a wooden handle, with which the dye can be applied.

claims.text: For woollen Kutch Bandhani lodki, sulphuric acid is used instead of acetic acid in dyeing.

quotes.quote: Sulphuric acid is used instead of acetic acid for dyeing.
The Vankar (weaver) community weaves woollen "lodki" (women's Veil cloth) in Adhoi, Bhachau Taluka.

claims.text: The woollen lodki is dyed red, a brightened colour being used for a bride's suhagadi lodki and maroon for the satbhateli lodki.

quotes.quote: after washing, the "lodki" is dyed in red colour, for the suhagadi (bride) lodki brightened colour is used where as for "Satbhateli lodki" maroon colour is used.

claims.text: The Vankar weaving community weaves the woollen lodki, a women's veil cloth, in Adhoi in Bhachau taluka.

quotes.quote: The Vankar (weaver) community weaves woollen "lodki" (women's Veil cloth) in Adhoi, Bhachau Taluka.

claims.text: On the lodki a grid is drawn with a cotton cord and the filling design is printed with blocks in a fugitive black colour.

quotes.quote: After dyeing, the design is printed on it with the help of a fugitive black colour. Here block printing and hand-drawing technique is used.
First the grid is drawn with the help of a cotton cord, and the filling design is printed with blocks.

claims.text: A lodki is tied in a single layer by women, and tying one, with 1800 to 2000 kadi, takes two or three days.

quotes.quote: The lodki is tied in a single layer. Two or three days are spent for tying one lodki which has 1800 to 2000 kadi. The tying is done by the women.

claims.text: After all the designs are tied, the lodki is dyed in black acid colour, washed and dried, and the tying is then opened.

quotes.quote: After tying all the designs, the material is dyed in black acid colour, then washed and dried. The tying is then opened up.

claims.text: The GI application lists Kutch Bandhani patterns including Chanderkhani, Shikari, Abha, Bagido, Ambadaal, Ras-Mandal, Bar-Bhag, Veerbut, Kamadia and Sangharia.

quotes.quote: There are different types of patterns available in Kutch Bandhani like Chanderkhani, Shikari, Abha , Bagido, Ambadaal, Ras-Mandal, Bar-Bhag, Veerbut, Kamadia, Sangharia etc.

claims.text: Khatri brides wear a black-ground bandhani whose central moon-shaped medallion gives it the name chandrokhani, meaning moon-like.

quotes.quote: Khatri brides wear a black background with the central moon-shaped medallion that gives the textile its name, Chandrokhani;
The large odhanis have similar patterns, with large central medallions against a black ground, which give them the name chandrokhani or 'moon-like'.

claims.text: In a chandrokhani a big circular motif called gul sits in the centre, and a wavy snake border called nag ni sar or sarpvel runs along the borders.

quotes.quote: The basic motifs used in Chandrokani are - in the center there is a big circular motif called gul and in the borders a wavy line called - Nag ni Sar or Sarpvel which means snake boarder.

claims.text: Chandrokhani was earlier red dots on a black ground with a red border and golden zari, but other colours are now also used.

quotes.quote: Earlier Chandrokhani was in red dots with black ground, and red pallu (Border) with golden zari, but now other colours are also used.

claims.text: Red and black are traditionally associated with the bridal costumes of the Khatri Muslim community of Kutch.

quotes.quote: This headscarf or coverlet is in the red and black traditionally associated with the bridal costumes of the Khatri Muslim community.
The black and red colour scheme is reminiscent of the tie-dyed clothing of the Khatri Muslims of Kutch.

claims.text: The khombi, a bandhani shawl traditionally red and black with white dotted patterns, is worn by brides of the Khatri and Muslim communities in Gujarat.

quotes.quote: A khombi shawl is worn by brides of the Khatri and Muslim communities in Gujarat. It is made using the bandhani technique and is traditionally red and black with white dotted patterns.
Khatri brides wear silk khombi veils with zari work on the border.

claims.text: The bavanbagh, or 52 gardens, and the rasamandali, associated with the Raas dance, have patterned red backgrounds with contrasting borders.

quotes.quote: Other traditional Bandhani include the Bavanbagh (the 52 gardens) and the Rasamandali (associated with Raas, the traditional dance form of Gujarat), both of which have patterned red backgrounds teamed with contrasting borders
Other traditional bandhani designs from Gujarat include the bavanbagh and the rasamandali, in which motifs such as mango trees, peacocks and elephants are also prevalent.

claims.text: In the ambadaal, or mango-branch design, the mango tree symbolises fertility, the elephant wealth and a woman carrying a water pot auspiciousness.

quotes.quote: Ambadaal means mango branches. In this design motifs like mango leaves and branches, along with elephants and statue of woman carrying water pot are also used. The mango tree is the symbol of fertility, elephant signifies wealth, woman carrying water pot signifies auspiciousness.

claims.text: Bar-bhag, meaning twelve parts, is a pattern of diagonal checks in which each rhombus carries a motif of ritual symbolism.

quotes.quote: Bar-bhag means twelve parts. It is a pattern formed by diagonal checks in the ground and each rhombus has a motif of ritual symbolism.

claims.text: The veerbut sari, a brother's gift to his sister on Raksha Bandhan, is always deep green, a colour that signifies growth, prosperity and fertility.

quotes.quote: Veerbut (Veer Bhet Bhat): It is a brother's gift to sister on the occasion of Raksha Bandhan. This traditional design sari is always in deep green colour which signifies growth, prosperity and fertility.

claims.text: A gharchola is a sari woven with gold or silver zari thread and embellished with bandhani that a man gives his bride, whose tie-dyed veil is called a chunri.

quotes.quote: A Gharchola is a saree woven with gold or silver zari thread and embellished with Bandhani that a man gives his bride, and the tie-dyed veil worn by the bride is known as a Chunri.

claims.text: For many women the bandhani sari is a symbol of married life, regarded as an article of great splendour that promises the bride a good future.

quotes.quote: The Bandhani saree, one of many tie and dye garments is a symbol of married life for many women. It is regarded as an article of great splendour that promises the bride a good future.

claims.text: The social, economic and cultural connotations of a bandhani are set by its base fabric, its design and its links with festivals and rites such as marriage and death.

quotes.quote: the social, economic and cultural connotations of a particular Bandhani is determined by the base fabric (gajji silk, fine cotton, muslin or wool), the design and its associations with festivals and rites of passage such as marriages and death.

claims.text: The quality of bandhani craftsmanship is judged by the contours, or kaff, of its dots and by the uniformity of their size and spacing.

quotes.quote: The quality of the craftsmanship can be judged by the contours or kaff of the dots formed, as well as by the uniformity of their size and spacing.

Traditional bandhani designs are valued based on the execution of this technique - patterns with numerous small and closely spaced dots are preferred to those with fewer, widely spaced or irregular dots.

claims.text: Kutch tie-and-dye cloth can be stitched into the abha, a women's upper garment whose yoke-like front, the agho, is tied and dyed up to the side.

claims.text: The GI application names red, yellow, green and blue as the traditional colours of bandhani.

quotes.quote: Red, yellow, green and blue are more efficient and traditional colors particularly to Bandhani.
Red, yellow, green and blue are traditional colours particularly to bandhani.

claims.text: The GI application's method of production gives yellow, red, blue, green and black as the main colours used in bandhani.

quotes.quote: The main colours used in Bandhana are yellow, red, blue, green and black.

quotes.quote: The entire cloth is then dipped in boiling dye for several minutes, washed and left to sun-dry. The small quantities of dye in the tied portions leak away while the concentrated dye in the surrounding cloth remains.

claims.text: After dyeing, the cloth is dried without opening its folds, because opening it while damp could damage it where air pockets may be trapped in the knots.

claims.text: After drying, the cloth is pulled forcibly crosswise so that all the ties open at once and the tie-threads lie on the material in a loose mass.

is done when two ends of the material are pulled crosswise tightly, loosening and opening the ties to reveal the colours and patterns in the fabric.

claims.text: In preparing the material, the cloth for Kutch Bandhani is carefully examined for quality and, if necessary, bleached.

quotes.quote: The raw materials required for Kutch Bandhani is carefully examined for its quality and if necessary, the cloth/fabric is bleached.

lede.text: Kutch Bandhani is a dyeing technique in which cloth is tied in intricate patterns with thread so that the tied areas resist the dye and leave dot-like designs.
It is a registered geographical indication for Kutch district of Gujarat, where bandhani is mainly practised by the Khatri community.
Bhuj, Mandvi, Anjar and Mundra produce cotton bandhani for contemporary use, and the GI application names its intricate designs and Rai Dana, or mustard-seed, dots as what makes it unique.

sentences.text: The GI application states that bandhani artisans are mostly immigrants from Sindh who came before Independence, and the Impart encyclopedia says the technique was originally practised by the Khatri community in Sindh.

The GI application cites Ajanta cave paintings of the 6th century AD showing women in blouses with dotted tie-dye patterns, and Bana's Harshacharita describing textiles being tied at the wedding of the prince's sister.

From the 12th century Jain script paintings of Western India show dotted garments that seem to be tie-dye, and a Gujarat writer of around AD 1373 used the expression chundi navarangiya for multicoloured bandhani.
The GI application cites a 15th-century Gujarat text as confirming that Mandvi in Kutch was renowned for dyeing odhanis.
In the 18th century the export of bandhani bandannas to Europe through the English East India Company made bandhani a staple local source of income.
Dyeing had hitherto been the Khatri community's domain in Kachchh; weavers began working directly with Khatris around the 1970s, and Bhadali and Moti Virani emerged as main bandhani centres.
Cloth that has been bleached is folded and its design is marked out in dots, through pinholes in a plastic sheet with an ink of geru, or traditionally with wooden blocks.
For tying, the cloth is folded into four or more layers, and tiny sections are pinched or raised and bound with strong thread, generally by women.
Sources differ on whether tiers use a fingernail or metal ring, and on how long tying takes: 4 to 90 days in the GI application, or a few days to many months according to Khamir.

After tying, the cloth is bleached, rinsed and dyed with chemicals swirled in hot water, and dyeing, which may be repeated for each colour starting with the lightest shade, continues until the desired colour combination is achieved.
A border is coloured by wrapping the tied cloth tightly in plastic bound with a rubber strip and scrubbing the dye into the material by hand.
Khamir describes washing the dyed cloth gently with soft water to remove any extra dye or impurities.
The cloth is dried without opening its folds and is then pulled forcibly crosswise so that all the ties open at once.
Bandhani is often sold with its knots still tied, so the customer can be sure it is not a printed imitation.
Bandhani artisans used local natural resources such as madder and pomegranate, and most Kutch Bandhani cloth was earlier the maroon of alizarin derived from madder.
Vat and naphtha dyes are used for cotton and acid dyes for silk, and synthetic dyes are affordable while bright colours are expensive and difficult to produce.
Sources differ on dyes: the GI application also states that the colours used are natural, and the use of natural dyes such as madder roots and pomegranate has seen a revival.
Chemical colours are never used directly because crystals could get caught in the material, and fast dyes that can be applied cold allow individual parts to be dyed by hand with felt.
The printing paste used to mark the designs for tying is of washable direct dyes.
Kutch Bandhani is prepared on cotton, silk, wool, georgette, tussar and rayon, and silk work uses gajji, a satin-weave silk, along with chiffon, chinon and mulberry silk.
The fineness of the tying depends on the fineness and texture of the material.
Fabric is procured from outside Kutch, from places such as Madurai, Bangalore, Varanasi and Surat; in 1971 the cloth, colours and thread were procured from the local market.
The 1971 gazetteer lists utensils for dyeing and wooden blocks for printing designs as the only tools and equipment needed.
The GI application defines the geographical area of production of Kutch Bandhani as Kutch district of Gujarat.
Sources differ on the area: the GI application also states that Kutch Bandhani is produced in Saurashtra, mainly in Jamnagar city.
Bandhani on cotton for contemporary use is produced in Mandvi, Mundra, Anjar and Bhuj, and the GI application, citing Veronica Murphy, says Mandvi is still an important tie-and-dye centre.

The GI application says Bhuj is well known for its red bandhani, and that dyeing is carried out extensively there as the water of the area is known to give a particular brightness to reds and maroons.
Cotton tie-dye for the Jat community is produced in Nani-Virani in Lakhpat taluka, and the woollen lodki is woven by the Vankar community in Adhoi in Bhachau taluka.
Kachchhi Khatri Bandhani Hastkala Association applied on 26 April 2021 to register Kutch Bandhani as a geographical indication, and certificate number 576 was issued on 30 March 2024.
The GI registry numbers its authorised users of Kutch Bandhani up to 67.
The 1971 Kutch District Gazetteer recorded bandhani giving whole or part-time employment to 4,000 persons.
Sources differ on how many women work in the craft: a 2019 report on Kachchh counts about 25,000 women in 350 tie-dye units, while an IRCI case study estimates about 15,000 in Kutch.
In 1971 a cotton bandhani cost Rs. 10 to Rs. 50 and a georgette one Rs. 50 to Rs. 250, and a bandhani's price depends on its cloth, design, colours and knots.

The 1971 gazetteer noted mechanised screen and roller printing as a rival to bandhani, and the GI application says technological advancement and synthetic dyes have raised competition and reduced prices.
Besides the Khatri community, women of the Jain, Harijan, Darji, Kumbhar, Jat, Mansuri and Rajput communities tie cotton Kutch Bandhani, and tying is paid in kadis of four dots.
The brothers Abduljabbar and Abdullah Khatri founded SIDR Craft in 1992 to revive high-quality bandhani, and Adil and Zakiya Khatri run Nilak, a design company producing Kutchi tie-dye products.
Kutch Bandhani has a style of dots and a style of lines called laheria, and its quality is judged by the contours, or kaff, of the dots and the uniformity of their size and spacing.
Red and black are traditionally associated with Khatri Muslim bridal costumes; Khatri brides wear the chandrokhani, a black ground with a central moon-shaped medallion.
The khombi, traditionally red and black with white dotted patterns, is worn by brides of the Khatri and Muslim communities in Gujarat.
Other designs include the bavanbagh of 52 gardens, the rasamandali, the ambadaal of mango branches and the bar-bhag of twelve parts.
The deep green veerbut sari is a brother's gift to his sister on Raksha Bandhan, and the gharchola is a sari embellished with bandhani that a man gives his bride.
Sources differ on colours: the 1971 gazetteer gives red, green, blue and black, while the GI application names red, yellow, green and blue as traditional.
